exercises.title: Print Working Directory (Wassim's pick)
exercises.instructions: Write the command to print your current working directory.
exercises.explanation: `pwd` prints the path of the current working directory.

exercises.title: Identify Current User
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display the username of the currently logged-in user.
exercises.explanation: `whoami` prints the effective username.

exercises.title: Show Date and Time
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display the current date and time.
exercises.explanation: `date` displays the system date and time.

exercises.title: View Command History
exercises.instructions: Write the command to show a numbered list of previously executed commands.
exercises.explanation: `history` displays the command history list.

exercises.title: Manual Page Access
exercises.instructions: Write the command to open the manual page for the `ls` command.
hints: Use `man` followed by the command name.
exercises.explanation: `man` displays manual pages for commands.

exercises.title: Absolute Path Concept
exercises.instructions: What type of path starts explicitly with the root slash `/`?
hints: It gives the full path from root.
exercises.explanation: An absolute path starts from the root directory `/`.

exercises.title: Inode Metadata
exercises.instructions: Write the command to list files along with their inode numbers in the current directory.
exercises.explanation: `ls -i` displays the inode number of each file.

exercises.title: Parent Directory Reference
exercises.instructions: In relative pathing, what symbol represents the parent directory?
exercises.explanation: `..` refers to the parent directory.

exercises.title: Current Directory Reference
exercises.instructions: What symbol represents the current directory in relative paths?
exercises.explanation: `.` represents the current working directory.

exercises.title: List Inode Numbers Explicitly
exercises.instructions: Write the command to list file names with their inode numbers in long format.
exercises.explanation: `ls -li` combines long listing with inode numbers.

exercises.title: Display Current User ID
exercises.instructions: Write the command to print your user ID and group IDs.
exercises.explanation: `id` prints user and group IDs.

exercises.title: Combine Short Options
exercises.instructions: Write a command to list all files (including hidden ones) in long format for the `/etc` directory by combining `-l` and `-a` into a single combined option string.
hints: Combine flags after a single dash.
exercises.explanation: Short options can be combined after a single dash like `-la`.

exercises.title: Repeat Last Command
exercises.instructions: Write the shell shorthand symbol used to repeat the immediately preceding command.
exercises.explanation: `!!` repeats the last command.

exercises.title: Line Continuation
exercises.instructions: Which symbol is used at the very end of a line to continue a command onto the next line?
exercises.explanation: A backslash `\` at the end of a line continues the command on the next line.

exercises.title: Command Separator
exercises.instructions: Write a single-line command sequence using a semicolon to change directory to `/tmp` and then list its contents.
exercises.explanation: Semicolon `;` runs multiple commands sequentially on one line.

exercises.title: Brace Expansion Creation
exercises.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression with `touch` to create three files named `log1.txt`, `log2.txt`, and `log3.txt` in one command.
exercises.explanation: Brace expansion `{1..3}` generates sequential strings `log1.txt log2.txt log3.txt`.

exercises.title: Directory Tree Brace Expansion
exercises.instructions: Write a command using `mkdir -p` and brace expansion to create a directory structure `project/src`, `project/docs`, and `project/tests` all at once.
exercises.explanation: `mkdir -p project/{src,docs,tests}` creates the base directory and three subdirectories simultaneously.

exercises.title: Comment Symbol
exercises.instructions: Which symbol starts a comment in a shell script or command line, ignoring the rest of the line?
exercises.explanation: `#` starts a comment; everything after it on the line is ignored.

exercises.title: Conditional Success Operator
exercises.instructions: Which operator runs the next command only if the previous command succeeded?
exercises.explanation: `&&` runs the subsequent command only upon success of the preceding one.

exercises.title: Exit Shell
exercises.instructions: Write the command or shortcut key sequence to exit the current shell session.
exercises.explanation: Typing `exit` or pressing `Ctrl+D` exits the shell.

exercises.title: History Number Execution
exercises.instructions: Write the command to re-run history command number 25.
hints: Exclamation mark followed by the number.
exercises.explanation: `!n` executes command number `n` from history.

exercises.title: Echo Variable
exercises.instructions: Write an `echo` command to print the value of a shell variable `USER`.
exercises.explanation: `echo $USER` prints the value of `USER`.

exercises.title: Long Options Prefix
exercises.instructions: Write the standard prefix formatting (number of dashes) for long options in Linux commands.
exercises.explanation: Long option names start with two dashes (`--`).

exercises.title: Repeat with Sudo
exercises.instructions: Write a shortcut command to re-run the previous command prefixed with `sudo`.
hints: Combine `sudo` with the repeat last command shortcut.
exercises.explanation: `sudo !!` re-runs the last command with root privileges.

exercises.title: Brace Expansion Letters
exercises.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression to echo letters `a`, `b`, and `c` separated by spaces.
exercises.explanation: `echo {a..c}` prints `a b c` via brace expansion.

exercises.title: Alternative Conditional Operator
exercises.instructions: Which operator runs the next command only if the previous command failed?
exercises.explanation: `||` executes the right-hand command only if the left-hand command fails.

exercises.title: Match Any Characters
exercises.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern to match any filename ending in `.txt`.
hints: Use `*` for any number of characters.
exercises.explanation: `*` matches any number of characters, including none.

exercises.title: Match Single Character
exercises.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern to match `file1.txt`, `file2.txt`, etc., where exactly one single character replaces the question mark in `file?.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `?` matches any single character.

exercises.title: Character List Bracket
exercises.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern using brackets to match files starting with `a`, `b`, or `c` followed by anything.
exercises.explanation: `[abc]*` matches names starting with `a`, `b`, or `c` followed by any characters.

exercises.title: Negated Bracket Wildcard
exercises.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern to match any filename starting with any character except digits 0 through 9.
hints: Use `!` or `^` inside brackets for negation.
exercises.explanation: `[!0-9]*` or `[^0-9]*` matches files not starting with a digit.

exercises.title: Digit Range Wildcard
exercises.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern to match `log3.txt` using a digit range `[0-9]` inside brackets.
exercises.explanation: `log[0-9].txt` matches log files with a single digit number.

exercises.title: Hidden Files Globbing
exercises.instructions: True or False: Standard wildcards like `*` match leading dots, so they automatically match hidden files without explicit notation.
hints: Hidden files start with a dot '.' which is ignored by standard `*`.
exercises.explanation: `*` and `?` do not match a leading dot; hidden files require explicit dot notation.

exercises.title: Zero-Padded Brace Expansion
exercises.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression to generate `01`, `02`, and `03`.
exercises.explanation: `{01..03}` generates zero-padded numbers.

exercises.title: Letter Range Brace Expansion
exercises.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression to generate letters `a` through `c`.
exercises.explanation: `{a..c}` expands to `a b c`.

exercises.title: Comma Brace Expansion
exercises.instructions: Write a brace expansion expression to generate `file1.txt` and `file2.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `file{1,2}.txt` generates `file1.txt file2.txt`.

exercises.title: List Log Files Glob
exercises.instructions: Write a `ls` command using a wildcard to list all `.log` files in the current directory.
exercises.explanation: `ls *.log` lists all files ending in `.log`.

exercises.title: Match Specific Range
exercises.instructions: Write a wildcard pattern matching any single lowercase letter from `a` to `z` followed by `.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `[a-z].txt` matches a single lowercase letter filename ending in `.txt`.

exercises.title: Touch Brace Log Files
exercises.instructions: Write a `touch` command using brace expansion to create `log1.txt`, `log2.txt`, and `log3.txt`.
exercises.explanation: Creates three files using brace expansion.

exercises.title: List Files Starting with Letter
exercises.instructions: Write an `ls` command using a wildcard to list files starting with `a`.
exercises.explanation: `ls a*` lists files starting with `a`.

exercises.title: List Single Character Extension
exercises.instructions: Write an `ls` command using `?` to list files named `fileX.txt` where `X` is any single character.
exercises.explanation: `ls file?.txt` matches a single character position.

exercises.title: Match Zero or More
exercises.instructions: Which wildcard symbol matches any number of characters, including zero characters?
exercises.explanation: `*` matches zero or more characters.

exercises.title: Change Directory Home
exercises.instructions: Write the command to change your current directory to your home directory.
exercises.explanation: `cd` or `cd ~` navigates to the user's home directory.

exercises.title: Go Back Previous Directory
exercises.instructions: Write the command to return to the previous directory you were in.
exercises.explanation: `cd -` switches back to the previous working directory.

exercises.title: Go Up Parent Directory
exercises.instructions: Write the command to move up one directory level.
exercises.explanation: `cd ..` moves to the parent directory.

exercises.title: List Long Format
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` command to list directory contents in long format.
exercises.explanation: `ls -l` shows permissions, link counts, owners, sizes, and timestamps.

exercises.title: List Hidden Files
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` command to show all files including hidden files starting with a dot.
exercises.explanation: `ls -a` shows all files including hidden ones and `.` / `..`.

exercises.title: List Directory Itself
exercises.instructions: Write the command to list the attributes and details of the `/etc` directory itself rather than its contents.
exercises.explanation: `ls -d` lists the directory itself rather than its contents.

exercises.title: Recursive Listing
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` option that recursively lists all contents of subdirectories.
exercises.explanation: `ls -R` lists subdirectory contents recursively.

exercises.title: Human Readable Sizes
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` option that displays file sizes in human-readable format (e.g., 4.0K, 2.3M).
exercises.explanation: `-h` makes file sizes human-readable when used with `-l`.

exercises.title: Sort by Time
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` option to sort files by modification time, newest first.
exercises.explanation: `-t` sorts the `ls` output by modification time.

exercises.title: Print Date Format
exercises.instructions: Write the `date` command option to format output as `YYYY-MM-DD` (using `%F`).
exercises.explanation: `date +%F` prints the date in ISO format (`YYYY-MM-DD`).

exercises.title: Quit Manual Page
exercises.instructions: What key do you press to quit out of a `man` manual page view?
exercises.explanation: Pressing `q` quits the `man` page viewer.

exercises.title: Search in Man Page
exercises.instructions: Which symbol/character do you type inside `man` to start searching for text?
exercises.explanation: Typing `/` followed by search terms allows searching inside `man` and `less`.

exercises.title: Root Directory Path
exercises.instructions: Write the command to change your directory to the topmost root directory `/`.
exercises.explanation: `cd /` navigates to the root directory.

exercises.title: Combined Listing Options
exercises.instructions: Write an `ls` command that combines long format, hidden files, and human-readable sizes.
exercises.explanation: `ls -lah` combines long format, all hidden files, and human-readable sizes.

exercises.title: List One Per Line
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` option to output exactly one entry per line.
exercises.explanation: `-1` forces single-column output in `ls`.

exercises.title: List Reverse Order
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` option to reverse the sorting order.
exercises.explanation: `-r` reverses the sort order.

exercises.title: Show Disk Allocation
exercises.instructions: Write the `ls` option to show the disk space allocated to each file in blocks.
exercises.explanation: `-s` displays file size allocation in blocks.

exercises.title: Navigation MCQ Concept
exercises.instructions: Which command prints the absolute path of the current working directory?
exercises.explanation: `pwd` prints the full path of the current directory.

exercises.title: List Specific Path
exercises.instructions: Write an `ls` command to list the contents of `/var/log` in long format.
exercises.explanation: `ls -l` lists specified directory paths.

exercises.title: Sort by Time Reverse
exercises.instructions: Write an `ls` command combining long format and sorting by modification time newest first.
exercises.explanation: `ls -lt` lists files in long format sorted by modification time.

exercises.title: Check File Type
exercises.instructions: Write the command to determine the type of a file named `document.pdf`.
exercises.explanation: `file` reports the classification and type of a file.

exercises.title: View Metadata Stat
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display detailed metadata (size, inode, permissions, timestamps) for `notes.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `stat` displays detailed low-level file metadata and timestamps.

exercises.title: Print Entire File
exercises.instructions: Write the command to print the entire contents of `notes.txt` to the terminal screen.
exercises.explanation: `cat` outputs the complete contents of files.

exercises.title: View First Lines
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display the first 5 lines of `notes.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `head -n 5` prints the first 5 lines of a file.

exercises.title: View Last Lines
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display the last 20 lines of `logfile.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `tail -n 20` prints the final 20 lines of a file.

exercises.title: Follow Log File
exercises.instructions: Write the `tail` command option that continuously follows and outputs new lines appended to a growing log file.
exercises.explanation: `tail -f` keeps the stream open and outputs new lines as they are appended.

exercises.title: Page by Page Viewer
exercises.instructions: Write the command to inspect a large file page by page with bi-directional scrolling and search capability.
exercises.explanation: `less` is a pager allowing backward and forward navigation through files.

exercises.title: Count Lines Words Bytes
exercises.instructions: Write the command to count the number of lines, words, and bytes in `notes.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `wc` reports newline, word, and byte counts.

exercises.title: Count Lines Only
exercises.instructions: Write the command to count strictly the number of lines in `notes.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `wc -l` outputs only the line count.

exercises.title: Byte vs Character Count
exercises.instructions: Which `wc` option counts bytes, and which option counts characters for non-ASCII text?
exercises.explanation: `wc -c` counts bytes while `wc -m` counts characters.

exercises.title: Join Multiple Files
exercises.instructions: Write a `cat` command that combines and prints the contents of `a.txt` and `b.txt` together.
exercises.explanation: `cat` can concatenate and print multiple files sequentially.

exercises.title: Head First Ten
exercises.instructions: Write a `head` command to print the first 10 lines of `data.txt` explicitly.
exercises.explanation: `head` prints the first lines of files.

exercises.title: Quit Less Pager
exercises.instructions: Write the key pressed inside `less` or `man` to quit the view.
exercises.explanation: `q` quits `less`.

exercises.title: Tail Last Ten
exercises.instructions: Write a `tail` command to print the last 10 lines of `data.txt` explicitly.
exercises.explanation: `tail` prints the final lines of files.

exercises.title: Command Comparison
exercises.instructions: Which inspection command allows scrolling both forward and backward through a file?
hints: Name implies it's more versatile than `more`.
exercises.explanation: `less` allows bidirectional navigation whereas `more` is mainly forward-only.

exercises.title: Create Directory
exercises.instructions: Write the command to create a new directory named `archive`.
exercises.explanation: `mkdir` creates new directories.

exercises.title: Create Parent Directories
exercises.instructions: Write the `mkdir` command option that creates missing parent directories automatically without failing if they exist.
exercises.explanation: `mkdir -p` creates parent directories as needed and suppresses errors if they exist.

exercises.title: Create Empty File
exercises.instructions: Write the command to create an empty file named `empty.txt` or update its timestamp.
exercises.explanation: `touch` creates an empty file or updates timestamps of existing files.

exercises.title: Copy File
exercises.instructions: Write the command to copy `source.txt` to `backup.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `cp` copies files from source to destination.

exercises.title: Copy Directory Recursively
exercises.instructions: Write the `cp` command option required to copy an entire directory recursively.
exercises.explanation: `cp -r` copies directories recursively.

exercises.title: Interactive Copy Prompt
exercises.instructions: Write the `cp` command option that prompts the user before overwriting an existing file.
exercises.explanation: `cp -i` prompts before overwriting existing files.

exercises.title: Move or Rename File
exercises.instructions: Write the command to rename `old.txt` to `new.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `mv` moves or renames files and directories.

exercises.title: Interactive Move Prompt
exercises.instructions: Write the `mv` command option to prompt before overwriting files.
exercises.explanation: `mv -i` prompts before overwriting.

exercises.title: Remove File
exercises.instructions: Write the command to delete a file named `temp.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `rm` deletes files permanently.

exercises.title: Remove Directory Recursively
exercises.instructions: Write the command with options to delete a directory named `old_dir` and all its contents recursively.
exercises.explanation: `rm -r` deletes directories and their contents recursively.

exercises.title: Force Remove
exercises.instructions: Write the `rm` command option to force removal without prompting or error messages.
exercises.explanation: `rm -f` forces deletion without prompting.

exercises.title: Remove Empty Directory
exercises.instructions: Write the command specifically used to remove an **empty** directory.
exercises.explanation: `rmdir` removes empty directories only.

exercises.title: Copy Multiple into Dir
exercises.instructions: Write a `cp` command to copy `a.txt` and `b.txt` into an existing directory `backup/`.
hints: List sources followed by target directory.
exercises.explanation: `cp` places multiple source files into the specified destination directory.

exercises.title: Move into Directory
exercises.instructions: Write a `mv` command to move `report.txt` into the `docs/` directory.
exercises.explanation: `mv` moves the file into the target directory.

exercises.title: Recycle Bin Warning
exercises.instructions: True or False: Linux command-line deletion via `rm` moves deleted files to a temporary desktop recycle bin.
exercises.explanation: Linux command-line `rm` permanently unlinks files; there is no recycle bin.

exercises.title: Create Multiple Empty
exercises.instructions: Write a `touch` command to create two empty files `one.txt` and `two.txt` simultaneously.
exercises.explanation: `touch` accepts multiple filenames to create or update them.

exercises.title: Nested Mkdir
exercises.instructions: Write a `mkdir` command to create `project/src/core` in a single command.
exercises.explanation: `mkdir -p` builds nested directory trees in one go.

exercises.title: Copy Directory Command
exercises.instructions: Write the complete command to copy directory `dir1` to `dir2` recursively.
exercises.explanation: `cp -r` copies directory trees recursively.

exercises.title: Interactive Rm
exercises.instructions: Write the `rm` command option that asks for confirmation before deleting each file.
exercises.explanation: `rm -i` prompts the user before removing files.

exercises.title: Touch Update Timestamp
exercises.instructions: Write a `touch` command to update the modification timestamp of `existing.txt` without changing its contents.
exercises.explanation: `touch` updates access and modification timestamps.

exercises.title: Echo Text
exercises.instructions: Write the `echo` command to print `Hello World` to standard output.
exercises.explanation: `echo` prints text to standard output.

exercises.title: Echo Escape Sequences
exercises.instructions: Write the `echo` option that enables interpretation of backslash escape sequences like `\n` (newline).
exercises.explanation: `echo -e` interprets backslash escapes like newlines and tabs.

exercises.title: Cut Fields Column
exercises.instructions: Write a `cut` command to extract the first column/field from `/etc/passwd` using `:` as the delimiter.
hints: Use `-d:` for delimiter and `-f1` for field 1.
exercises.explanation: `cut -d: -f1` extracts field 1 using colon delimiter.

exercises.title: Sort Numerically
exercises.instructions: Write the `sort` command option to sort numbers in numerical order rather than alphabetical order.
exercises.explanation: `sort -n` sorts numerically so 9 comes before 10.

exercises.title: Sort Reverse
exercises.instructions: Write the `sort` command option to reverse the sort order.
exercises.explanation: `sort -r` reverses the sorting order.

exercises.title: Uniq Count Occurrences
exercises.instructions: Write the `uniq` command option to prefix each unique line with its count of occurrences.
exercises.explanation: `uniq -c` prefixes lines with their repetition count (requires sorted input).

exercises.title: Uniq Duplicate Lines
exercises.instructions: Write the `uniq` command option to output only lines that are duplicated.
exercises.explanation: `uniq -d` outputs only repeated lines.

exercises.title: Tr Translate Lower Upper
exercises.instructions: Write a `tr` command to translate all lowercase letters to uppercase from standard input.
exercises.explanation: `tr` translates characters from set1 to set2.

exercises.title: Tr Delete Characters
exercises.instructions: Write the `tr` command option to delete given characters from input.
exercises.explanation: `tr -d` deletes specified characters.

exercises.title: Tee Command Save
exercises.instructions: Write a command using `tee` to save standard output to `output.txt` while also displaying it on screen.
exercises.explanation: `tee` copies stdin to stdout and files simultaneously.

exercises.title: Tee Append Option
exercises.instructions: Write the `tee` command option to append to the file instead of overwriting it.
exercises.explanation: `tee -a` appends output to the target file.

exercises.title: Sort Requirement for Uniq
exercises.instructions: True or False: `uniq` only collapses **consecutive** duplicate lines, so sorting the input first is typically required.
exercises.explanation: `uniq` only detects adjacent duplicate lines, requiring `sort` beforehand.

exercises.title: Process Status Ps
exercises.instructions: Write the `ps` command with `aux` options to list all running processes in user-oriented format.
exercises.explanation: `ps aux` displays all running processes across all users.

exercises.title: Sed Simple Substitution
exercises.instructions: Write a `sed` command to replace the first occurrence of `foo` with `bar` in `file.txt` (without editing in place).
exercises.explanation: `sed 's/foo/bar/'` substitutes the first match per line.

exercises.title: Sed Global Substitution
exercises.instructions: Write a `sed` command to replace **all** occurrences of `foo` with `bar` on every line of `file.txt` using the global flag.
exercises.explanation: `sed 's/foo/bar/g'` replaces all occurrences on each line.

exercises.title: Sed In-Place Editing
exercises.instructions: Write the `sed` command option for editing a file **in place** on GNU/Linux.
exercises.explanation: `sed -i` modifies files directly in place.

exercises.title: Sort Unique Option
exercises.instructions: Write the `sort` command option to output only unique lines (removing duplicates).
exercises.explanation: `sort -u` sorts and removes duplicate lines.

exercises.title: Sort Numeric Flag
exercises.instructions: Write a `sort` command to sort `numbers.txt` in numeric order.
exercises.explanation: `sort -n` sorts numerically.

exercises.title: Tr Squeeze Option
exercises.instructions: Write the `tr` command option to squeeze repeated character sequences into a single occurrence.
exercises.explanation: `tr -s` squeezes sequences of repeated characters.

exercises.title: Sed Print Lines
exercises.instructions: Write a `sed` command using `-n` and `p` to print only lines 5 through 10 of `file.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `sed -n '5,10p'` suppresses default printing and prints lines 5 to 10.

exercises.title: Stdout Overwrite
exercises.instructions: Write a command to redirect standard output of `ls` into `list.txt`, overwriting the file.
exercises.explanation: `>` redirects stdout, overwriting the destination file.

exercises.title: Stdout Append
exercises.instructions: Write a command to append the output of `date` to `log.txt` without overwriting existing content.
exercises.explanation: `>>` appends stdout to the destination file.

exercises.title: Stderr Redirection
exercises.instructions: Write a command to redirect standard error of a command `/nonexistent` into `error.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `2>` redirects standard error (file descriptor 2).

exercises.title: Discard Errors
exercises.instructions: Write a redirection syntax to discard all standard error messages by sending them to `/dev/null`.
exercises.explanation: `2>/dev/null` discards error output.

exercises.title: Redirect Both Stdout Stderr
exercises.instructions: Write a Bash shorthand command to redirect both standard output and standard error of `make` into `build.log`.
exercises.explanation: `&>` redirects both stdout and stderr to a file in Bash.

exercises.title: Stdin Redirection
exercises.instructions: Write a command using `<` to sort contents of `unsorted.txt` and save to `sorted.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `<` redirects a file into standard input of a command.

exercises.title: Pipe Connector
exercises.instructions: Write a command using a pipe to count the number of entries listed by `ls`.
hints: Pipe symbol `|` connects stdout to stdin.
exercises.explanation: `ls | wc -l` pipes stdout of `ls` into `wc -l` to count lines.

exercises.title: Stream Descriptors
exercises.instructions: What is the numeric file descriptor number for standard error?
exercises.explanation: Standard error is file descriptor 2.

exercises.title: Dev Null Purpose
exercises.instructions: What special file acts as a bit bucket that discards everything written to it?
exercises.explanation: `/dev/null` discards all output written to it.

exercises.title: Stderr to Stdout Syntax
exercises.instructions: Write the standard syntax fragment `2>&1` meaning what?
exercises.explanation: `2>&1` merges standard error into standard output.

exercises.title: Pipe vs Redirection
exercises.instructions: True or False: A pipe (`|`) connects the stdout of one command to the stdin of another command, whereas redirection connects a command to a file.
exercises.explanation: Pipes connect commands; redirection connects files.

exercises.title: Combine Stderr and Stdout Portable
exercises.instructions: Write the portable command syntax to send both stdout and stderr of `cmd` to `out.txt` without using `&>`.
exercises.explanation: `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` is the standard portable way to redirect both streams.

exercises.title: Stdin Descriptor
exercises.instructions: What is the numeric file descriptor number for standard input?
exercises.explanation: Standard input is 0.

exercises.title: Stdout Descriptor
exercises.instructions: What is the numeric file descriptor number for standard output?
exercises.explanation: Standard output is 1.

exercises.title: Overwrite Warning
exercises.instructions: True or False: Using `>` empties the target file before the command runs.
exercises.explanation: `>` truncates the file.

exercises.title: Create Symbolic Link
exercises.instructions: Write the command to create a symbolic (soft) link named `soft.txt` pointing to `target.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `ln -s` creates a symbolic link.

exercises.title: Create Hard Link
exercises.instructions: Write the command to create a hard link named `hard.txt` pointing to `target.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `ln` creates a hard link sharing the same inode.

exercises.title: Inode Sharing Concept
exercises.instructions: True or False: A hard link shares the exact same inode number as the original file.
hints: Hard links point directly to the inode.
exercises.explanation: Hard links point directly to the underlying inode and data.

exercises.title: Symbolic Link Target Type
exercises.instructions: True or False: A symbolic link stores a path (text) pointing to the target, whereas a hard link points directly to an inode.
exercises.explanation: Symlinks store paths.

exercises.title: Cross Filesystem Hard Link
exercises.instructions: True or False: Hard links can span across different disk partitions and file systems.
exercises.explanation: Hard links cannot cross filesystems.

exercises.title: Directory Hard Link Restriction
exercises.instructions: True or False: Standard users can create hard links to directories.
exercises.explanation: Users cannot hard-link directories.

exercises.title: Original Deleted Soft Link
exercises.instructions: What happens to a symbolic link if its original target file is deleted?
exercises.explanation: Deleting the target breaks the symbolic link.

exercises.title: Original Deleted Hard Link
exercises.instructions: What happens to a hard link if its original filename is deleted?
exercises.explanation: The data remains accessible via the hard link.

exercises.title: Symlink Directory Creation
exercises.instructions: Write a command using `ln -s` and `-t` (GNU) to create a symbolic link inside `/tmp/links` pointing to `/etc/hosts`.
exercises.explanation: `ln -s -t dir target` creates a symlink inside `dir`.

exercises.title: List Inode Command
exercises.instructions: Which `ls` option displays inode numbers alongside files to inspect hard links?
exercises.explanation: `ls -i` displays inode numbers.

exercises.title: Link Indicator in Ls
exercises.instructions: When listing files with `ls -l`, what letter starts the permissions string for a symbolic link?
exercises.explanation: Symbolic links start with `l`.

exercises.title: Link Definition
exercises.instructions: What does an inode store?
exercises.explanation: An inode stores file metadata.

exercises.title: Single Quote Behavior
exercises.instructions: True or False: Single quotes `' '` prevent all shell expansions, including variable expansion and wildcards.
hints: Single quotes preserve literal values strictly.
exercises.explanation: Single quotes disable variable expansion and wildcard interpretation entirely.

exercises.title: Double Quote Behavior
exercises.instructions: True or False: Double quotes `" "` allow variable expansion and command substitution while preventing wildcard expansion.
exercises.explanation: Double quotes permit variables.

exercises.title: Variable in Double Quotes
exercises.instructions: Given `name="Alice"`, what does `echo "Hello $name"` output?
exercises.explanation: Double quotes evaluate `$name` to `Alice`.

exercises.title: Variable in Single Quotes
exercises.instructions: Given `name="Alice"`, what does `echo 'Hello $name'` output?
exercises.explanation: Single quotes treat `$name` literally.

exercises.title: Filename with Spaces
exercises.instructions: Write a command to create a single file named `my file.txt` with a space using quotes.
exercises.explanation: Quotes allow filenames containing spaces to be treated as a single argument.

exercises.title: Prevent Wildcard Expansion
exercises.instructions: Write a command using quotes around `*` so `echo` literally prints an asterisk `*` instead of expanding filenames.
exercises.explanation: Quoting `*` prevents the shell from expanding it as a glob.

exercises.title: Single Quote Escaping
exercises.instructions: True or False: A single-quoted string can contain a literal single quote inside it if you just use standard typing.
exercises.explanation: Cannot embed single quotes directly.

exercises.title: Backslash Escape Single
exercises.instructions: Write how to escape a single quote inside single quotes or use backslash outside quotes to print `it's`.
hints: Close quotes, insert escaped quote, reopen.
exercises.explanation: Requires quote concatenation.

exercises.title: Command Substitution Quoting
exercises.instructions: True or False: Command substitution `$(cmd)` is evaluated inside double quotes but not inside single quotes.
exercises.explanation: Evaluated inside double quotes.

exercises.title: Best Quote for Regex
exercises.instructions: Which quotation type is best for regex patterns and `sed`/`awk` scripts to prevent shell interference?
exercises.explanation: Single quotes prevent shell expansion.

exercises.title: Wildcard Globbing Quote
exercises.instructions: Why must pattern arguments in commands like `find -name "*.txt"` be quoted?
exercises.explanation: Quoting prevents shell expansion.

exercises.title: Quote Purpose Summary
exercises.instructions: What is the primary purpose of quoting in the shell?
exercises.explanation: Controls shell expansions.

exercises.title: Switch User
exercises.instructions: Write the command to switch user account to `bob` starting a full login shell.
exercises.explanation: `su - bob` switches to user bob with a login shell environment.

exercises.title: Sudo Switch User
exercises.instructions: Write a `sudo` command to start a login shell as `bob` using your own sudo rights.
exercises.explanation: `sudo -i -u bob` starts a login shell as bob using sudo.

exercises.title: Create User Home
exercises.instructions: Write the `useradd` command option to automatically create the user's home directory.
exercises.explanation: `useradd -m` creates the user's home directory.

exercises.title: Delete User Home
exercises.instructions: Write the `userdel` command option to remove the user's home directory and mail spool.
exercises.explanation: `userdel -r` deletes the user account and home directory.

exercises.title: Add User to Group
exercises.instructions: Write the `usermod` command option to **add** a user to supplementary groups while keeping existing ones.
exercises.explanation: `usermod -aG group user` appends supplementary groups safely.

exercises.title: Create Group
exercises.instructions: Write the command to create a new group named `developers`.
exercises.explanation: `groupadd` creates a new system group.

exercises.title: Show User Groups
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display the groups to which the current user belongs.
exercises.explanation: `groups` prints group memberships.

exercises.title: Show User ID
exercises.instructions: Write the command to show UID, primary GID, and all group memberships for a user.
exercises.explanation: `id` displays user and group IDs.

exercises.title: Change Password
exercises.instructions: Write the command to change your own password.
exercises.explanation: `passwd` updates user authentication passwords.

exercises.title: Passwd File Path
exercises.instructions: Which file stores basic account and user information, one line per user?
exercises.explanation: `/etc/passwd` stores account info readable by everyone.

exercises.title: Shadow File Path
exercises.instructions: Which file stores encrypted password hashes and aging data, readable only by root?
exercises.explanation: `/etc/shadow` holds hashes.

exercises.title: Sudoers Editor
exercises.instructions: What is the mandatory safe tool used to edit `/etc/sudoers` configuration files?
exercises.explanation: `visudo` edits sudoers safely.

exercises.title: Lock Password
exercises.instructions: Write the `usermod` option to lock a user's password.
exercises.explanation: `usermod -L` locks passwords.

exercises.title: Unlock Password
exercises.instructions: Write the `usermod` option to unlock a user's password.
exercises.explanation: `usermod -U` unlocks passwords.

exercises.title: Password Aging Chage
exercises.instructions: Write the `chage` command option to display password aging and expiration info for a user.
exercises.explanation: Lists aging info.

exercises.title: Force Password Change
exercises.instructions: Write a `chage` command to force a user to change their password at next login by setting last change date to 0.
exercises.explanation: Forces password change.

exercises.title: Noninteractive Chpasswd
exercises.instructions: Write a command using `chpasswd` to set a user password non-interactively via pipe.
exercises.explanation: Updates password non-interactively.

exercises.title: Root UID Number
exercises.instructions: What is the numeric User ID (UID) of the root superuser account?
exercises.explanation: Root UID is 0.

exercises.title: Group File Path
exercises.instructions: Which file stores group definitions and member lists?
exercises.explanation: Group file path.

exercises.title: Newgrp Command
exercises.instructions: What does the `newgrp` command do?

accepted: Starts a new shell with new primary group

exercises.explanation: Switches primary group in a new shell.

exercises.title: Chmod Numeric 755
exercises.instructions: Write a `chmod` command using octal notation to set permissions `755` on `script.sh`.
exercises.explanation: `chmod 755` sets owner rwx, group r-x, and others r-x.

exercises.title: Chmod Symbolic Add Execute
exercises.instructions: Write a `chmod` command using symbolic notation to add execute permission for the owner on `script.sh`.
exercises.explanation: `chmod u+x` adds execute permission for the user owner.

exercises.title: Chmod Remove Group Write
exercises.instructions: Write a `chmod` command using symbolic notation to remove write permission from the group on `file.txt`.
exercises.explanation: `chmod g-w` removes write permission from the group.

exercises.title: Numeric Octal Values
exercises.instructions: In octal permission values, what numerical value represents read (`r`)?
exercises.explanation: Read `r` equals 4, write `w` equals 2, execute `x` equals 1.

exercises.title: Numeric Write Value
exercises.instructions: In octal permissions, what numerical value represents write (`w`)?
exercises.explanation: Write is 2.

exercises.title: Numeric Execute Value
exercises.instructions: In octal permissions, what numerical value represents execute (`x`)?
exercises.explanation: Execute is 1.

exercises.title: Chown Command Owner
exercises.instructions: Write the command to change the owner of `file.txt` to `alice`.
exercises.explanation: `chown` changes file ownership.

exercises.title: Chown Owner and Group
exercises.instructions: Write the command to change the owner of `file.txt` to `alice` and group to `developers` simultaneously.
exercises.explanation: `chown user:group` updates both owner and group at once.

exercises.title: Chgrp Command
exercises.instructions: Write the command to change only the group ownership of `file.txt` to `developers`.
exercises.explanation: `chgrp` changes group ownership.

exercises.title: Umask Display
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display the current umask value.
exercises.explanation: `umask` displays permission mask bits subtracted from defaults.

exercises.title: Directory Execute Meaning
exercises.instructions: Write the meaning of execute (`x`) permission on a directory.

accepted: Permission to enter and access items inside

exercises.explanation: Execute on a directory permits entering (`cd`) and traversing it.

exercises.title: Sticky Bit Purpose
exercises.instructions: What is the primary purpose of the sticky bit on a shared directory like `/tmp`?

accepted: Prevents users from deleting files they do not own

hints: Prevents users from deleting each other's files.
exercises.explanation: The sticky bit prevents users from deleting files they do not own.

exercises.title: SUID Bit Meaning
exercises.instructions: What does SUID do when set on an executable file?
exercises.explanation: SUID executes the program with the privileges of the file's owner.

exercises.title: SGID Directory Meaning
exercises.instructions: What does SGID do when set on a directory?
exercises.explanation: New files inherit the directory's group owner.

exercises.title: Sticky Bit Octal
exercises.instructions: What leading octal digit represents the sticky bit when setting permissions with `chmod` (e.g., `1777`)?
exercises.explanation: Sticky bit is `1`.

exercises.title: SUID Bit Octal
exercises.instructions: What leading octal digit represents the SUID bit?
exercises.explanation: SUID is `4`.

exercises.title: SGID Bit Octal
exercises.instructions: What leading octal digit represents the SGID bit?
exercises.explanation: SGID is `2`.

exercises.title: Recursive Chmod
exercises.instructions: Write a `chmod` command to set permissions `750` recursively on `myfolder/`.
exercises.explanation: `chmod -R` applies permission changes recursively.

exercises.title: Private File Octal
exercises.instructions: What octal permission mode `NNN` is typically used for private files like SSH private keys (`rw-------`)?
exercises.explanation: `600` for private files.

exercises.title: Private Directory Octal
exercises.instructions: What octal permission mode `NNN` is typically used for private directories (`rwx------`)?
exercises.explanation: `700` for private directories.

exercises.title: Default File Umask 022
exercises.instructions: If the umask is `022`, what default permission do new regular files receive?
exercises.explanation: New files receive `644`.

exercises.title: Default Dir Umask 022
exercises.instructions: If the umask is `022`, what default permission do new directories receive?
exercises.explanation: New directories receive `755`.

exercises.title: Delete File Requirement
exercises.instructions: To delete a file within a directory, what permission do you need on the **parent directory**?
exercises.explanation: Requires write and execute on parent directory.

exercises.title: Set Umask Value
exercises.instructions: Write the command to set the umask to `027` for the current shell session.
exercises.explanation: Sets umask.

exercises.title: Chgrp Alternative
exercises.instructions: Write a `chown` command syntax to change only the group owner of `file.txt` to `staff` using a colon prefix.
exercises.explanation: Changes group only.

exercises.title: Find by Name
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search your home directory `~` for files named `*.txt` (ensure pattern is quoted).
exercises.explanation: `find ~ -name "*.txt"` searches home directory for matching names.

exercises.title: Find by Type Directory
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search the current directory `.` for directories only (`-type d`).
exercises.explanation: `find . -type d` locates directories.

exercises.title: Find by Type File
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search `/var` for regular files only (`-type f`).
exercises.explanation: `find /var -type f` locates regular files.

exercises.title: Find by Owner
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search root `/` for files owned by user `alice` (suppressing permission errors).
exercises.explanation: `find / -user alice 2>/dev/null` searches files owned by alice.

exercises.title: Find Modified Days Ago
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search your home directory for files modified more than 7 days ago (`-mtime +7`).
exercises.explanation: `find ~ -mtime +7` finds files modified over 7 days ago.

exercises.title: Find Modified Minutes Ago
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search your home directory for files modified within the last 10 minutes (`-mmin -10`).
exercises.explanation: `find ~ -mmin -10` finds files modified in the last 10 minutes.

exercises.title: Find Size Greater Than
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search `/` for files larger than 100 MiB (`-size +100M`, hiding errors).
exercises.explanation: `find / -size +100M 2>/dev/null` finds large files exceeding 100 MiB.

exercises.title: Find Exact Permissions
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command to search your home directory for regular files with exact permissions `644`.
exercises.explanation: `find ~ -type f -perm 644` locates files matching exact permissions.

exercises.title: Find Max Depth Option
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command option to limit search depth to a maximum of 1 directory level.
exercises.explanation: `-maxdepth 1` restricts search to the immediate directory level.

exercises.title: Find Exec Action
exercises.instructions: Write a `find` command snippet using `-exec` to execute `rm` on every found `.tmp` file.
exercises.explanation: `-exec cmd {} \;` runs the given command on each search result.

exercises.title: Numeric Argument Plus Meaning
exercises.instructions: In `find` numeric arguments, what does `+n` mean (e.g., `-mtime +7`)?
exercises.explanation: `+n` means strictly greater than `n`.

exercises.title: Numeric Argument Minus Meaning
exercises.instructions: In `find` numeric arguments, what does `-n` mean (e.g., `-mmin -10`)?
exercises.explanation: `-n` means strictly less than `n`.

exercises.title: Find Type Code File
exercises.instructions: What single-letter type code represents a regular file in `find -type t`?
exercises.explanation: `-type f` specifies regular files.

exercises.title: Find Type Code Directory
exercises.instructions: What single-letter type code represents a directory in `find -type t`?
exercises.explanation: `-type d` specifies directories.

exercises.title: Find Wildcard Quoting
exercises.instructions: Why must `-name` wildcard patterns like `"*.txt"` be quoted when using `find`?
exercises.explanation: Quoting prevents shell expansion.

exercises.title: Tar Create Gzip
exercises.instructions: Write a `tar` command to create a compressed gzip archive named `backup.tar.gz` from `myfolder/`.
exercises.explanation: `tar -czf` creates a gzip-compressed tar archive.

exercises.title: Tar Extract Gzip
exercises.instructions: Write a `tar` command to extract a gzip tar archive named `backup.tar.gz` in the current directory.
exercises.explanation: `tar -xzf` extracts a gzipped tar archive.

exercises.title: Tar List Contents
exercises.instructions: Write a `tar` command to list the contents of `backup.tar.gz` without extracting it.
exercises.explanation: `tar -tf` lists archive contents.

exercises.title: Tar Extract to Directory
exercises.instructions: Write a `tar` command option (`-C dir`) to extract an archive into a specific target directory `/tmp/restore`.
exercises.explanation: `-C dir` changes directory before extracting files.

exercises.title: Tar Compression Flags
exercises.instructions: Which `tar` option specifies gzip compression?
exercises.explanation: `-z` compresses or decompresses using gzip.

exercises.title: Tar Bzip2 Flag
exercises.instructions: Which `tar` option specifies bzip2 compression?
exercises.explanation: `-j` uses bzip2 compression.

exercises.title: Tar Xz Flag
exercises.instructions: Which `tar` option specifies xz high compression?
exercises.explanation: `-J` uses xz compression.

exercises.title: Scp Remote Copy
exercises.instructions: Write an `scp` command to copy a local file `report.txt` to a remote user `alice` at host `192.168.1.10` into `/home/alice/`.
exercises.explanation: `scp` copies files securely over SSH using `user@host:path` notation.

exercises.title: Scp Recursive Directory
exercises.instructions: Write the `scp` command option required to copy an entire directory remotely.
exercises.explanation: `scp -r` copies directories recursively.

exercises.title: Tar Create Flag
exercises.instructions: Which `tar` operation flag specifies creating a new archive?
exercises.explanation: `-c` creates a new tar archive.

exercises.title: Tar Extract Flag
exercises.instructions: Which `tar` operation flag specifies extracting an archive?
exercises.explanation: `-x` extracts files from an archive.

exercises.title: Scp Remote Source
exercises.instructions: Write an `scp` command to copy a remote file `/home/alice/report.txt` from `alice@192.168.1.10` to the current local directory `.`.
hints: Remote source followed by local destination `.`.
exercises.explanation: `scp` supports copying from remote to local by specifying remote source first.

exercises.title: Tar File Flag Placement
exercises.instructions: True or False: In `tar`, the `-f` flag must be placed last among option clusters, directly followed by the archive filename.
hints: `-f` requires the filename argument immediately after.
exercises.explanation: `-f` must immediately precede the archive filename argument.

exercises.title: Tar Uncompressed Create
exercises.instructions: Write a `tar` command to create an uncompressed archive named `archive.tar` from `folder/`.
exercises.explanation: `tar -cf` creates an uncompressed tar archive.

exercises.title: Scp Port Option
exercises.instructions: What capital option letter is used in `scp` to specify a non-default SSH port?
exercises.explanation: `-P` specifies a custom remote SSH port in `scp`.

exercises.title: Config Directory Path
exercises.instructions: Which standard top-level directory stores system-wide configuration files?
exercises.explanation: `/etc` holds system configuration files.

exercises.title: Temporary Directory Path
exercises.instructions: Which standard directory stores temporary files and is world-writable with the sticky bit?
exercises.explanation: `/tmp` stores temporary files.

exercises.title: Variable Logs Directory
exercises.instructions: Which standard directory stores variable data including system logs in `/var/log`?
exercises.explanation: `/var` stores variable data such as logs, databases, and mail spools.

exercises.title: Home Directory Path
exercises.instructions: Which standard directory contains user home directories?
exercises.explanation: `/home` contains individual user home directories.

exercises.title: Root Home Directory
exercises.instructions: What is the home directory path for the `root` superuser?
exercises.explanation: `/root` is the superuser's home directory.

exercises.title: Binaries Directory
exercises.instructions: Which standard directory stores standard user executable commands (often a link to `/usr/bin`)?
exercises.explanation: `/bin` and `/usr/bin` store standard user commands.

exercises.title: Device Files Directory
exercises.instructions: Which standard directory contains device files representing hardware and special files like `/dev/null`?
exercises.explanation: `/dev` contains device files representing hardware and virtual streams.

exercises.title: Boot Files Directory
exercises.instructions: Which standard directory stores Linux kernel and boot loader files?
exercises.explanation: `/boot` stores bootloader and kernel image files.

exercises.title: Runtime State Directory
exercises.instructions: Which directory stores runtime state information since boot (PID files, sockets)?
exercises.explanation: `/run` holds volatile runtime state data since system boot.

exercises.title: Etc Passwd Purpose
exercises.instructions: What specific file inside `/etc` stores basic user account records?
exercises.explanation: `/etc/passwd` holds user account records.

exercises.title: Root Filesystem Purpose
exercises.instructions: What does the root slash `/` represent in the Linux filesystem hierarchy?
exercises.explanation: `/` is the root directory.

exercises.title: Log Files Location
exercises.instructions: Where are system log files typically located within `/var`?
exercises.explanation: `/var/log` is the log directory.

exercises.title: Create Local Variable
exercises.instructions: Write the shell syntax to create a local shell variable named `GREETING` with value `hello` (no spaces around `=`).
exercises.explanation: `NAME=value` assigns a local shell variable.

exercises.title: Export Environment Variable
exercises.instructions: Write the command to export a shell variable `GREETING` so it becomes available to child processes.
exercises.explanation: `export` makes variables available to child processes as environment variables.

exercises.title: Print Environment Variables
exercises.instructions: Write the command to display all current environment variables.
exercises.explanation: `env` and `printenv` list environment variables.

exercises.title: Path Variable Purpose
exercises.instructions: What environment variable defines the colon-separated list of directories searched for executable commands?
exercises.explanation: `PATH` specifies directories searched when executing commands.

exercises.title: Create Command Alias
exercises.instructions: Write a command to create an alias named `ll` that shortcuts to `ls -la`.
exercises.explanation: `alias` creates shortcut commands.

exercises.title: Remove Alias
exercises.instructions: Write the command to remove an alias named `ll`.
exercises.explanation: `unalias` removes defined command aliases.

exercises.title: Bashrc File Path
exercises.instructions: What is the name of the per-user Bash configuration file located in the home directory?
exercises.explanation: `~/.bashrc` is the standard per-user interactive Bash config file.

exercises.title: Source Bashrc
exercises.instructions: Write the command to reload your `~/.bashrc` configuration file in the current shell session without restarting.
exercises.explanation: `source ~/.bashrc` re-reads and applies configuration changes immediately.

exercises.title: Path Append Syntax
exercises.instructions: Write a command to append a directory `~/bin` to the existing `PATH` variable correctly.
exercises.explanation: `export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/bin"` appends a directory to search paths.

exercises.title: Show Path Variable
exercises.instructions: Write an `echo` command to print the contents of the `PATH` environment variable.
exercises.explanation: Prints search paths.

exercises.title: Enter Insert Mode
exercises.instructions: Which key pressed in Normal mode enters Insert mode so you can type text in Vim?
exercises.explanation: Pressing `i` enters Insert mode in Vim.

exercises.title: Return to Normal Mode
exercises.instructions: Which key do you press to return to Normal mode from Insert mode in Vim?
exercises.explanation: Pressing `Esc` returns to Normal mode.

exercises.title: Save and Quit Command
exercises.instructions: What command-line mode command saves changes and quits Vim simultaneously?
hints: Colon followed by w and q.
exercises.explanation: `:wq` saves and quits Vim (or `ZZ` in Normal mode).

exercises.title: Quit Discard Changes
exercises.instructions: What command-line mode command quits Vim immediately discarding any unsaved changes?
hints: Colon followed by q and exclamation mark.
exercises.explanation: `:q!` forces quitting without saving changes.

exercises.title: Delete Line Command
exercises.instructions: What two-letter Normal mode command deletes (cuts) the current line in Vim?
exercises.explanation: `dd` deletes the current line in Normal mode.

exercises.title: Yank Line Command
exercises.instructions: What two-letter Normal mode command yanks (copies) the current line in Vim?
exercises.explanation: `yy` copies (yanks) the current line.

exercises.title: Paste Command
exercises.instructions: What key in Normal mode pastes previously yanked or deleted text after the cursor?
exercises.explanation: `p` pastes text after the cursor or on the line below.

exercises.title: Undo Command
exercises.instructions: What single key in Normal mode undoes the last change in Vim?
exercises.explanation: `u` undoes the previous edit.

exercises.title: Go to First Line
exercises.instructions: What two-letter Normal mode command jumps to the very first line of the file?
exercises.explanation: `gg` jumps to the first line of the file.

exercises.title: Go to Last Line
exercises.instructions: What single Normal mode command key jumps to the very last line of the file?
exercises.explanation: `G` jumps to the last line of the file.

exercises.title: Search Forward
exercises.instructions: What symbol typed in Normal mode starts searching forward for text in Vim?
exercises.explanation: `/` initiates forward text searching in Vim.

exercises.title: Vim Modal Nature
exercises.instructions: True or False: Vim is a modal editor, meaning keys perform different functions depending on whether you are in Normal mode or Insert mode.
exercises.explanation: Vim operates using distinct modes (Normal, Insert, Command).

exercises.title: Redo Command
exercises.instructions: What key combination (`Ctrl + key`) redoes an undone change in Vim?
exercises.explanation: `Ctrl+r` performs redo in Vim.

exercises.title: Save Only Command
exercises.instructions: What command-line mode command saves (writes) changes without exiting Vim?
exercises.explanation: `:w` saves the file.

exercises.title: Open Line Below
exercises.instructions: What single Normal mode key opens a new line directly below the current line and enters Insert mode?
exercises.explanation: `o` opens a new line below and switches to Insert mode.
